When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Leilani had always been a meticulous person, but since the accident, her attention to detail had become an all-consuming force in her life. It had been two years since she was involved in a life-threatening car crash on her way home from work as a cybersecurity analyst. The memories of that night still haunted her - the sound of shattering glass, the smell of burning rubber, and the feeling of helplessness as she lay trapped in the wreckage. As she reflected on the accident, Leilani couldn't shake off the feeling that it was deeply unfair. She had always been a careful driver, and yet, fate had seen fit to deal her such a cruel blow. This sense of injustice gnawed at her, making her question everything about herself and the world around her. She felt exposed, as if others could see the trauma she had endured just by looking at her. Leilani became withdrawn, avoiding social interactions and public places where she might be forced to confront her fears. To cope with these feelings, Leilani developed a range of maladaptive strategies. She would ruminate on the accident, replaying every detail in her mind, trying to make sense of it all. She avoided anything that could trigger strong emotions - happy or sad - as she felt she was living on borrowed time. And when memories of the accident threatened to surface, Leilani tried to erase them from her mind, as if by willing them away, she could undo the damage. However, these strategies only served to fuel her sense of threat. Leilani found herself constantly on edge, scanning her surroundings for potential dangers, and waking up multiple times a night to check if she was safe. She became convinced that she couldn't trust her own body, that it had betrayed her in some fundamental way. This lack of trust made her hypervigilant, always waiting for the other shoe to drop. As Leilani struggled to sleep, memories of the accident would flood back - the visual images, the smells, and even the physical pain. These flashbacks left her feeling like she was reliving the trauma all over again. She began to see herself as vulnerable, exposed to the whims of fate, and this perception only reinforced her negative appraisals. In an attempt to regain some semblance of control, Leilani threw herself into her work as a cybersecurity analyst. However, even in this familiar territory, she found herself on high alert, constantly monitoring for potential threats. Her colleagues noticed a change in her, but Leilani just couldn't shake off the feeling that danger lurked around every corner. It was only when Leilani's relationships with her loved ones began to fray that she realized she needed help. She was tired of living in a state of constant vigilance, tired of being haunted by memories she couldn't erase. With a deep breath, Leilani made the decision to seek therapy, hoping to find a way to quiet the threat that had taken up residence in her mind and to rebuild a sense of trust in herself and the world around her. As she sat in her therapist's office for the first time, Leilani felt a glimmer of hope. Maybe, just maybe, she could learn to tame the fears that had been holding her hostage and find a way to live with the memories of that fateful night without being consumed by them.
